# SK7110 — The logger is declared for a different type than the one that declares it

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A type declares an ILogger<T> field, property or constructor parameter whose T is neither itself nor one of its base types.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Maintainability |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S3416, S6672 |

## Why

The type argument is the log *category*. A class holding an `ILogger<Other>` files every message it ever writes under another class's name, so a filter that selects this class misses them and a filter that selects the other one collects messages it never sent. Nothing fails, nothing is slow, and every log query about either class is quietly wrong — which is worse than noise, because noise is visible. The fix is mechanical: the category the declaration meant is the type the declaration is in. ⚠ **This is the objective quarter of issue #237, and the other three members are declined on purpose.** `S6669` (what the field is *named*) and `S1312` (whether it is `private static readonly`) are naming and declaration conventions, which are the most opinionated thing a linter can hold and a repository's to settle rather than a defect anybody can be shown. `S3416`'s `LogManager.GetLogger(typeof(Other))` shape is covered here only where the category is a declared `ILogger<T>`; Serilog's `Log.ForContext<T>()` is deliberately out, because choosing a context other than the enclosing type is a normal and intended use of that method rather than a mistake.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class OrderService {
    readonly ILogger<PaymentService> logger;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class OrderService {
    readonly ILogger<OrderService> logger;
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A base type of the declaring type is accepted.** A hierarchy that files its whole family under the base class's category is a deliberate grouping, and the type argument still names something whose declaration the reader can find. Only an unrelated type is reported. ⚠ **Fields, properties and constructor parameters only** — the places a type *keeps* a logger. A `typeof(ILogger<Other>)`, a local in a composition root, a factory's return type and a method parameter that forwards one all name another class's logger on purpose, and reporting them would turn a rule about one type's own category into a rule against dependency injection. ⚠ **A type parameter is never reported**: `ILogger<T>` inside a generic helper is a category decided at the use site, not a wrong one, and there is no name a fix could write in its place. Comparison is on original definitions, so `Repository<T>` holding an `ILogger<Repository<T>>` is correct and the fix writes the type parameter list back. ⚠ **`defaultSeverity` is `suggestion` rather than `none`, and the measured count that would have argued for `none` does not exist**: Skala's own tree contains no `ILogger<T>` declaration at all — the shape is absent, verified by grep and by a probe file that made the rule fire once inserted — so a Skala count cannot show the rule is noisy. What settles it is that the finding is not a preference: `SK7010` and `SK7101` ship at `none` because a reader may reasonably disagree with them, and nobody reasonably wants their messages filed under another class's name. Generated code is excluded.
